name: Gareth Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a rural crew for Brackenridge Power, out in farm country. Mostly we replace old wooden poles, some of them put in before I was born, and restring the lines between farms. I'm the groundman and an apprentice: I dig, I guide the auger truck, I fetch and carry, and I talk to the farmers about getting onto their land, because I was one of them for thirty years. I milked sixty cows on the family farm until I sold the herd at 55.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the early starts and the hedgerows and a day's honest work, same as farming. And I like that the farmers trust me, so the crew sends me to knock on the door when there's a bull in the field. What wears me out is the book learning. The written tests for the apprenticeship are hard for me, all formulas, and I've failed one already. My wife Ruth sits with me at the kitchen table and reads me the questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. I'm going to describe five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I thought as much. Most of these new things are clever men in cities selling each other ideas. I'd say it at the church hall after the service, and that'd be the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to finish what I started, God willing. Seven or eight years on the poles, a modest pension, and then the garden and the grandchildren. That's all I've ever wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just carry on. Resit my test in March, keep working, keep a bit aside each month. I'd not change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never used AI. Has anyone tried to get you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandson tried to put one on my phone at Christmas. I told him I've got a wife for advice and a Bible for the big questions. I'll not have a machine telling me what to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does money look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've about three months put by. The herd and the land went to clear the farm debts, so there's no fortune, but we rent a cottage cheap from the estate. Ruth keeps hens and sells eggs at the gate, which pays for the church collection and a bit over.

S0.say: He'd tell people at the church hall that he thought as much, describing AI as clever city people selling each other ideas.
S0.think: Privately he sees this as a chance to finish what he started, God willing: seven or eight years on the poles, a modest pension, then the garden and grandchildren.
S0.do: Carries on: resits his failed apprenticeship test in March, keeps working and puts a little aside each month. Changes nothing.
S0.quote: I told him I've got a wife for advice and a Bible for the big questions.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth's faith and family are the frame for everything he says, and he's openly unwilling to use AI. He came to line work after selling his dairy herd to clear debts. His value to the crew is his trust with farmers, while written tests are his weak spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the market sort it out. If a machine does a job better, fair enough, as long as nobody expects the taxpayer to prop up everyone it puts out of work. I'd also say a man should be ready to learn a new trade, like I did at 55.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think it comes near a wooden pole in a muddy field. The office might change, the meter readers might go. But somebody still has to walk out across the field and talk the farmer round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal and see what the company does before I fret. If they hand me a tablet, I'll learn the buttons I need, and Ruth can help. I wouldn't spend a penny on anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little wary, the way you watch a new dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a man should be ready to learn a new trade. But you'd only learn the buttons you need. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I learned a trade, poles and wires, because it's real work with my hands. A computer isn't a trade, it's a gadget. I'll learn a trade at any age, but I'll not chase every gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young lad on our crew, Owen, who's always on his phone. If his head's in the screen and the screen does his thinking, what's he got when it breaks? I'd tell him to learn to read a pole with his eyes.

S1.say: He'd say let the market sort it out, as long as taxpayers aren't expected to support everyone displaced, and that people should be ready to learn a new trade as he did at 55.
S1.think: Privately he doesn't think AI reaches a wooden pole in a muddy field. The office and meter readers might change, but someone still has to cross the field and talk the farmer round.
S1.do: Carries on and waits to see what the company does. Learns only the tablet buttons he needs, with his wife's help, and spends nothing on new things.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a little wary, like watching a new dog.
S1.quote: But somebody still has to walk out across the field and talk the farmer round.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth separates a trade, which he'll learn at any age, from gadgets, which he won't chase. His free-market line comes with a firm dislike of handouts. He sees his people skills with farmers as the part of the job no machine touches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big tech companies have run ahead of everybody, and they'll not be the ones paying for it. I'd say families and churches will have to pull together, because that's what's left when the big things fail. I'd not be marching anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be frightened for a bit. I'd be 60, a groundman with a half-finished apprenticeship and a farmer's back. I lost one way of life when the cows went, and I didn't think I'd lose another so soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut back to the bone, no trips, no new anything, and save every penny towards six months. I'd fix tractors and mowers for neighbours for cash, because farmers will still have old machines. And I'd talk to my son Daniel, who has his own electrical business, about labouring for him if the company lets me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray on it a good deal, and that helps me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd lean on Daniel. Would his business be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. If robots can wire a house, he's in trouble too. Then we'd be leaning on each other, and on the church. We did that in the bad milk years, and we got through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't much warning. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the house in order. Pay off the little loan on the van, put the eggs money aside, and start the repair work on Saturdays so it's going before I need it. You don't plant seed the week you're hungry.

S2.say: He'd blame the big tech companies for running ahead of everyone and say families and churches must pull together. He wouldn't march.
S2.think: Privately he'd be frightened: at 60, with a half-finished apprenticeship and a farmer's back, he'd face losing a second way of life soon after the first.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the bone and saves towards six months. Starts repairing neighbours' tractors and mowers for cash on Saturdays, pays off the van loan and asks his son about labouring for his electrical business.
S2.quote: You don't plant seed the week you're hungry.
S2.fieldNote: Gareth's fallbacks are family, church and his own practical skills, not the state, which fits his outlook. Faith keeps him at anxious rather than alarmed. He's realistic that his son's business may be hit too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for sensible people to get ready, and that's on them, not on the government. Young folk should get an apprenticeship in something the machines can't do. I'd say it plainly to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd be 63 and I'd have my ticket, God willing. I'd have the repair work going on the side. It would hurt, but it'd be a hard winter, not a lost farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, start the tractor repairs on Saturdays in a year or so, and put that money aside. I'd plan to stop on the poles at 63 if the machines came, and keep the repair work going after. We'd stay in the cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a long dry spell. You can plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your mind about using AI or the new tools in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd sooner do repairs by ear, the way my father did. If the farmers want robot tractors, they can call the dealer. I'll fix the old ones, and there'll be plenty of those for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family would you think about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Hannah's boys. The eldest is 12. I'd want him in a proper trade with a master who'll teach him, not stuck in front of a screen. I'd help pay for it if it came to that.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough for sensible people to prepare and that it's their responsibility, not the government's, urging young people towards apprenticeships machines can't do.
S3.think: Privately he expects to be 63 with his qualification and a repair business on the side. It would be a hard winter, not a lost farm.
S3.do: Finishes the apprenticeship, starts Saturday tractor repairs within a year and saves the income. Plans to stop line work at 63 if robots arrive and keep the repair work going afterwards.
S3.feel: Uneasy, like a long dry spell he can plan for.
S3.quote: It would hurt, but it'd be a hard winter, not a lost farm.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Gareth plan in farming terms: a hard winter rather than ruin. He stays firm against AI tools and bets on fixing old machines. His concern for the next generation is about real trades taught by a master.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who isn't ready by then has only themselves to blame. Families should help their own get ready. That's the old way, and it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's no great matter. I'd retire at 66 in 2034. What troubles me is what men do with their days when there's no work. Work is how a man looks after his family, and I don't know what a world without it does to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, finish the ticket, work to 66. Help Hannah's boys find apprenticeships in good trades. I might keep fixing tractors in the barn, just to keep my hands busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more for the grandchildren and the young men than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people without work worry you. What do you picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture the lads from our village sat at home on a handout with nothing to get up for. I saw it with farmers who lost their land: the drink, the quiet. A cheque isn't the same as a purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be safe yourself. Why does it trouble you so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'll be in the same church pew next to those families. You can't be content when your neighbours aren't. My father taught me that, and the Lord did before him.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty and anyone not ready has only themselves to blame, with families helping their own prepare in the old way.
S4.think: Privately he expects to retire at 66 in 2034, so it's no great matter for him. What troubles him is what people do without work, since he sees work as how a man looks after his family.
S4.do: Carries on, finishes his qualification and works to 66. Helps his grandsons find apprenticeships in good trades and keeps fixing tractors to stay busy.
S4.feel: Uneasy, more for the grandchildren and young men than for himself.
S4.quote: A cheque isn't the same as a purpose.
S4.fieldNote: Gareth's worry in the slow picture is moral, not financial: what idleness does to people. It comes from watching farmers who lost their land. He feels tied to his neighbours through church and won't be content if they suffer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be thrown off a second way of life at 60 with no time to get the repair work going. What would help is the company keeping on older men for the parts machines can't do, like dealing with farmers, and apprenticeships that are real, with a master, not courses on a screen. And families and churches doing what they've always done.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what people would do with their days. Everyone talks about money. My father milked cows until the week he died, and I think he'd have died sooner without them.

headlineQuote: My father milked cows until the week he died, and I think he'd have died sooner without them.
portrait: Gareth Fischer is a 58-year-old groundman and apprentice on a rural Brackenridge Power crew replacing old wooden poles in farm country, after thirty years milking sixty cows on his family farm. He's a churchgoer who leans on faith, family and free markets, dislikes handouts and won't have AI on his phone. He struggles with written tests but is the one the crew sends to talk farmers round. In the milder pictures he expects little to change for him. AGI in two years makes him anxious because he'd lose a second way of life at 60, so he'd cut back, start repairing tractors for cash and lean on family and church. With five or ten years he plans a hard winter rather than ruin, and worries most about what a world without work does to people.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because he'd lose a second way of life at 60 with no time to set up his repair work.
whatWouldHelp: His employer keeping older workers on for jobs machines can't do, real apprenticeships with a master, and families and churches supporting each other.
